subtype: Approach: letting go of a small item after a fair search [Revision]
passage: The maths test was tomorrow and Pooja could not find her sharpener. She turned out her bag and checked under the desk and looked along the window sill. She asked Kiran, who had not seen it, and then the girl in the next row. Ten minutes were gone. It was a plain, cheap sharpener, and her pocket money for the week was already spent. "This is not worth any more time," she told herself. She borrowed Kiran's, sharpened three pencils, and went back to the sums. That evening she scratched her name on the new one with a compass point.

qa.q: Who lent Pooja a sharpener?
qa.a: Kiran lent Pooja a sharpener.

qa.q: What was Pooja thinking when she said "This is not worth any more time"?
qa.a: She weighed how much time the search had already cost against how little the sharpener was worth. She felt tired of searching and decided to move on to the sums.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pooja try to stop losing sharpeners, and why?
qa.a: She could keep a small pouch inside her bag for her sharpener and eraser. Then things return to the same place and there is less to hunt for.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Pooja's problem?
qa.a: Kiran sees Pooja, who searched properly, asked and then chose not to waste any more of the evening before the test, so lending a sharpener is an easy way to help.

grounding: After a proper search and asking around, the girl decides a cheap sharpener is not worth more time, borrows one and marks her name on the next.

subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Salma dropped her bag on the sofa. "Mummy, I have so much homework!" Her mother Manjula sat down beside her. "Tell me what it is." "Sums. Then Hindi writing, one paragraph. Also a drawing." "How long will each take?" Salma looked at the ceiling. "Sums, ten minutes. No, twenty. The paragraph, um, ten. The drawing is thirty." She counted on her fingers. "Twenty and ten and thirty... that is one hour." She blinked. "Only one hour?" "Only one hour," said Manjula. Salma took a pencil and wrote the three tasks on a page.

qa.q: How long did Salma guess the drawing would take?
qa.a: She guessed the drawing would take thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when she found the total was one hour?
qa.a: She was surprised and relieved. Her blink and the words "Only one hour?" show the homework stopped seeming so big.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help if Salma still feels worried, and why?
qa.a: She could set a timer for each task and tick it off. Watching the list shrink shows her the work is really finishing.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Salma's list?
qa.a: Manjula sees a daughter who turned a heap of worry into three tasks she can count, and she only had to ask how long each would take.

grounding: A Class 5 child lists her tasks and estimates the minutes, and the one-hour total makes the work feel finite.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest subject first while fresh [Action]
passage: After his snack, Nitin opened his maths book at the kitchen table. "I'll do the word problems first," he told his mother Disha. "My head is fresh now." She nodded and went back to the dal. He read the first problem twice, drew a little diagram and worked it through. By the time the last one was done, the sun was low. The map for Social Studies was still waiting, a blank outline. He yawned, took out the crayons and started colouring the rivers blue, slow and easy, and the whole page was finished before dinner.

qa.q: What did Nitin do first after his snack?
qa.a: He started with the maths word problems.

qa.q: Why did Nitin choose the maths word problems first, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He felt fresh and confident, since he said his head was fresh, and he wanted the harder work done while he could think well.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nitin use if he still gets stuck on a word problem, and why?
qa.a: He could put a star next to it and ask his mother after the others. Getting stuck early would not eat the rest of his time.

qa.q: How does Disha see the way Nitin plans his homework?
qa.a: Disha sees a son who chooses his own order and needs no reminders. She can go on cooking and trust him to manage.

grounding: A boy does hard maths first, right after his snack when his head is clear, and saves the easy map colouring for when he is tired.

subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]
passage: After school, Noa spread her felt pens across the table in the flat in Toronto. She drew a fox for her poster, then copied out her spelling words in careful, curly writing. It felt nice, like play. At eight o'clock her father Bilal looked in. "How are the maths sums?" Noa's eyes were heavy. Only the hard sums were left, and her pencil slid across the page. She scribbled the answers fast to be done. The next morning the teacher's red marks showed four wrong, all careless slips.

qa.q: What did Noa do first with her felt pens?
qa.a: She drew a fox for her poster.

qa.q: What might Noa have been feeling at eight o'clock when only the hard sums were left?
qa.a: She was sleepy and tired, and probably a bit pressed to finish. Her eyes were heavy and she scribbled the answers fast.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Noa use tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: She could start with the hard sums while she is fresh and keep the drawing for later. Her best energy would go to the hardest task.

qa.q: How might Bilal see what happened that evening?
qa.a: Bilal asked about the sums at eight and saw a sleepy daughter with the hardest task left, so he may worry she saved the tough work for the end.

grounding: A girl finishes the drawing and copying she enjoys first, so at 8 pm only hard sums remain, she is sleepy and rushes them with mistakes.

subtype: Approach: pushing it off until just before bedtime [Pitfall]
passage: At the hostel study hour, Dev told himself there was plenty of time. He played cricket in the corridor with a rolled-up sock and watched cartoons in the common room. When the 9 o'clock bell rang, he opened his science file and saw the diagram of the digestive system. It would take an hour. His stomach dropped. Tears came, and he walked to the warden's room. "Bidisha Ma'am, I have not started." Bidisha sat with him, helped him see where to begin, and stayed while he drew the first outline. Lights out came before the labels were done.

qa.q: What was Dev doing instead of homework during study hour?
qa.a: He played cricket in the corridor and watched cartoons.

qa.q: What was Dev feeling when he opened the science file at 9 o'clock?
qa.a: He felt panicked and sad. His stomach dropped, tears came, and he went to the warden for help.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dev use another evening, and why?
qa.a: He could look at his homework first and put the longest task at the start. Then he would know how much time it really needs.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see Dev arriving at her room at that hour?
qa.a: Bidisha sees a child who is upset, not lazy, and who chose to ask for help. Bidisha sits with him while he begins.

grounding: A boy tells himself there is plenty of time, plays until 9 pm, then finds the diagram takes an hour, cries and asks an adult to help.

subtype: Approach: seeing the crowded evening and redoing the plan [Revision]
passage: Faisal had just started his sums when his mother Afreen came in. "Cousin Hafsa is coming at six." He looked at the clock and at the list, and then he saw the whole evening. Sums, reading, dinner, guests. He crossed out his first plan and wrote a new one: sums first, before dinner. Reading after the guests left. He worked quickly until the doorbell rang. Hafsa stayed for tea and stories. At nine, with the guests gone, Faisal opened his reader and finished the last page. Nothing was left undone.

qa.q: At what time was Cousin Hafsa coming?
qa.a: Hafsa was coming at six.

qa.q: What did Faisal feel when he looked at the clock and saw the whole evening?
qa.a: He felt a bit pressed and concerned that there would not be room for everything. He crossed out his first plan and started again.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Faisal use if the guests stay late, and why?
qa.a: He could read a little in the morning before school. That way the reading would not be lost and he would not need to stay up.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about visiting while Faisal has homework?
qa.a: Hafsa probably enjoys the tea and stories because Faisal has already finished his sums, so the visit is relaxed for both of them.

grounding: Halfway through his homework a boy notices a cousin is coming at 6 pm and redoes the plan, sums before dinner and reading after the guests leave.

subtype: Approach: working in short blocks with small breaks [Action]
passage: Monday. Binita took the kitchen timer from her mother Jyoti. She set it for twenty minutes and started her sums. When it rang she stopped, though she was in the middle of a line. She drank water and stretched her arms. Tuesday. She did the same with the reading. The second block felt lighter than the first. Wednesday. Three blocks of twenty minutes, with three breaks. The maths, the reading and the spelling were all finished by six o'clock. At dinner, Binita said, "I did not even feel it."

qa.q: How long did Binita's timer run for each block of work?
qa.a: It was set for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Binita feel at dinner when she said "I did not even feel it"?
qa.a: She felt pleased and a little surprised. The work seemed lighter because the breaks made each block easier.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Binita use on a day with a big project, and why?
qa.a: She could write the blocks on a list and tick each one after its break. Seeing ticks pile up helps her keep going.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see the timer being used?
qa.a: Jyoti lent the timer and now sees Binita managing her own time, with homework done before dinner, so there is no need to hurry her.

grounding: A child works in twenty-minute blocks with five-minute breaks using a kitchen timer, so the whole thing gets done before dinner.

subtype: Approach: working next to a sibling doing their own homework [Action]
passage: The TV was loud in the living room, so Neha carried her books to the kitchen table, where her older brother Manoj was studying. She opened her maths book and glanced at him. He was writing quietly, his pencil moving in steady strokes. She copied his quiet and picked up her own pencil. The clock ticked. She got through half a page without stopping. Then one problem would not budge. She waited a bit, tried again, and only then whispered, "Bhaiya, can you show me this one?" He looked at it and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Neha take her books to do her homework?
qa.a: She carried her books to the kitchen table.

qa.q: What was Neha feeling as she sat beside Manoj, and what does her progress suggest?
qa.a: She felt calm and focused. Seeing him work quietly made her want to work, and she got half a page done without stopping.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Neha use if Manoj is busy, and why?
qa.a: She could put a star next to the hard problem and do the rest first. Then she can ask him when he finishes his work.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Neha sitting next to him?
qa.a: Manoj is probably glad to have her there, quiet and busy, and does not mind being asked when she is really stuck. She waited before she whispered her question.

grounding: A girl works at the same table as her older brother, who is studying, and asks a question only when truly stuck.

subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage: I'm Bhavna, and my brother Pranav was doing fractions at the table last evening. He frowned at one question for a long time. About fifteen minutes passed, and he rubbed his eye and his pencil pressed harder. Then he stopped and drew a star beside the question. I don't know what he was thinking, but he closed his eyes for a moment. He walked over to our mother and said, "Amma, I'm stuck on this one." She sat with him for a few minutes. He went back to the other questions and finished them all.

qa.q: What did Pranav draw beside the question that he could not do?
qa.a: He drew a star beside it.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling before he drew the star?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and upset, since the question kept beating him. Bhavna saw that his pencil pressed harder and he rubbed his eye.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pranav try, and why?
qa.a: He could look back at a solved example in his notebook before asking. It may show him the step he missed.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see the moment Pranav asked for help?
qa.a: Bhavna could only watch, and saw him stop, close his eyes, and choose to ask. Bhavna does not know what Pranav felt, but he got back to the other questions.

grounding: A child stuck on a fractions question notices he is only getting upset, marks it with a star, asks his mother and moves on to the other questions.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage: Hemant looked at the window. His friends were already playing in the park below. He scribbled the last answers of his maths homework as fast as he could, slammed the notebook shut and ran out. The next day Devika Ma'am returned the books. Two sums had red crosses. "Look at question three, Hemant," she said quietly. He had written 48 where the book said 84, and in the other sum he had left out a zero. He stared at the page. A minute of checking would have caught both, and now he had lost the marks.

qa.q: Which sums did Devika Ma'am mark wrong?
qa.a: She marked two sums wrong, with red crosses.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he saw the two red crosses?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and annoyed with himself. He stared at the page because he knew he could have caught the errors.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Hemant use to check his work quickly, and why?
qa.a: He could read each answer once against the book before closing the notebook. A short check is enough to catch copying slips.

qa.q: How does Devika Ma'am see the two wrong sums?
qa.a: Devika Ma'am sees careless copying errors, not a gap in understanding. That is why she pointed calmly at question three.

grounding: A boy scribbles answers to go out and play and skips checking, so the next day the teacher marks two sums wrong for copying errors.
